findings.title: Release blockers remain open for signing, independent review, and cross-platform evidence
findings.observedBehavior: release/release-manifest.json sets releaseStatus to blocked with three unmet blockers: trusted-signing-identity, independent-security-review, and cross-platform-ci-evidence. The build produces an unsigned candidate, and scripts/build-release.mjs correctly refuses to treat it as a signed release.
findings.expectedBehavior: A distribution presented as production ready carries a trusted signature, an independent security review, and cross-platform continuous-integration evidence for every supported operating system and Node major.
findings.impact: Consumers cannot verify provenance or integrity of the distribution they receive, and no third party has reviewed the security posture. The gates are correctly implemented and correctly failing, so this is an outstanding process obligation rather than a defect, but it bounds how the release may be described.

evidence.description: releaseStatus is blocked with three named blockers and requireSignature and requireIndependentReview both true.
The build refuses to relax the internal distribution policy and produces an unsigned candidate only.
The release status block states the three open blockers explicitly rather than implying full assurance.

findings.resolution: Obtain a trusted signing identity and sign the candidate, commission and record an independent security review, and publish cross-platform CI evidence for Windows, Linux, and macOS on Node 22, 24, and 26. Clear each blocker in the manifest only when its evidence artifact exists and verifies.
verification: Run npm run release:verify against a signed candidate and confirm signature validation passes.
Confirm reports/cross-platform-ci-evidence.json covers every required operating system and Node major.
Confirm release/release-manifest.json lists no remaining blockers.
assumptions: The distribution remains restricted to authorized internal use until the blockers are cleared.

findings.title: Equivalence classification can suppress a framework standard that is broader than the project's own
findings.observedBehavior: findEquivalentAsset marks a scoped instruction as covered when an existing project file shares at least one applyTo glob and one significant purpose token. A short project-authored file can therefore suppress a substantially more detailed framework standard.
findings.expectedBehavior: Coverage suppression reflects genuine equivalence of guidance, not merely overlapping scope and vocabulary.
findings.impact: A repository can end up with weaker guidance than intended while the adoption plan reports the topic as covered. The consequence is bounded because every decision is printed with the covering path, mandatory templates are never suppressed, and --force-templates restores installation, but a reviewer who does not read the covered list may not notice.

evidence.description: Scoped instruction equivalence requires only one shared glob and one shared token.
Every covered decision is printed with its covering path and recorded in the adoption plan.
The clarification protocol is marked mandatory and is excluded from equivalence suppression.

findings.resolution: Add a coverage-depth signal such as relative content length or checklist-item count, and downgrade a match to a reported overlap rather than a suppression when the project's file is materially thinner. Continue to require explicit review of the covered list before apply.
verification: Adopt a fixture whose existing instruction is a single line and assert the framework template is reported as an overlap rather than suppressed.
Adopt a fixture whose existing instruction is comprehensive and assert suppression still occurs.
Confirm --force-templates continues to install regardless of classification.

findings.title: Stack detection is bounded and can under-report languages in very large repositories
findings.observedBehavior: detectProjectStack stops at a directory depth of 5 or after visiting 20000 entries, and skips common build output directories. A language present only below that depth or beyond that cap is not detected, so its scoped instruction file is not installed and its continuous-integration steps are not generated.
findings.expectedBehavior: Detection either covers the repository or reports that it stopped early so the user can supply the stack explicitly.
findings.impact: A large monorepo can silently receive fewer scoped standards than it needs. The bound exists deliberately to keep planning fast and is mitigated by an explicit stack declaration, but the truncation is currently invisible to the user.

evidence.description: SCAN_MAX_DEPTH is 5 and SCAN_MAX_ENTRIES is 20000, with no signal emitted when either limit is reached.
The adoption plan reports the detected stack but not whether the scan completed.

findings.resolution: Record whether either limit was reached, surface a truncated-scan notice in the adoption plan and printed summary, and accept a --stack override on the adopt command so a user can declare what detection missed.
verification: Construct a fixture that exceeds the entry cap and assert the plan reports a truncated scan.
Assert a declared stack on adopt installs the corresponding instruction files regardless of detection.
Confirm normal repositories report a complete scan.

findings.title: Generated pipelines for non-Node stacks depend on unpinned runner-provided tooling
findings.observedBehavior: continuousIntegrationWorkflow emits pinned actions only for checkout and Node setup. Python, .NET, Java, Go, Rust, Ruby, PHP, Bicep, and Terraform steps invoke tooling preinstalled on the GitHub-hosted runner image without pinning a version.
findings.expectedBehavior: Generated pipelines pin the toolchain version they depend on so a runner image change cannot silently alter or break the build.
findings.impact: A runner image update can change compiler or SDK versions under a project without any repository change, producing an unexplained build difference. This was a deliberate trade-off: emitting setup actions would have required commit SHAs that could not be verified at authoring time, and fabricating them would have been worse.

evidence.description: Only CHECKOUT_ACTION and SETUP_NODE_ACTION carry verified commit SHAs; other stacks use bare shell invocations.
The repository's own workflows are fully pinned to current verified SHAs, so the gap is limited to generated non-Node pipelines.
The repository's own workflows are fully pinned, so the gap is limited to generated non-Node pipelines.

findings.resolution: Add verified commit SHAs for the official setup actions of each supported stack, emit them alongside an explicit toolchain version, and extend the template pinning rule to cover generated workflow content as well as shipped template files. Resolve each SHA from the action repository with git ls-remote rather than transcribing a version tag, as was done for the checkout, setup-node, upload-artifact, and download-artifact bumps in this release.
verification: Assert every generated workflow references only actions pinned to a full commit SHA.
Assert each supported stack pins an explicit toolchain version.
Run a generated pipeline for at least one non-Node stack and confirm it succeeds.

findings.title: The runtime is a single large module with no automated hygiene tooling
findings.bugType: Module size and missing static analysis
findings.observedBehavior: pso.mjs is roughly 2300 lines in one module and contains several long functions, notably buildAdoptionPlan and createProject, that mix discovery, classification, content generation, and manifest construction. No linter, formatter, or complexity tool is configured in the repository.
findings.expectedBehavior: A production runtime is decomposed into focused modules with automated hygiene enforcement, so review effort scales with change size rather than file size.
findings.impact: Review and onboarding cost rises with every feature. The zero-dependency constraint that makes the distribution attractive also blocks the usual linting tooling, so hygiene currently depends entirely on the contract suite and manual inspection.

evidence.description: One module holds constants, detection, planning, transactions, verification, inventory, and the command-line interface.
No lint script is defined and no static analysis dependency is declared.

findings.resolution: Split the runtime into modules along existing seams such as detection, template planning, transactions, and inventory, keeping the single-file entry point. Add a hygiene gate that runs without third-party dependencies, or make a deliberate, documented exception to the zero-dependency rule for development-only tooling.
verification: Confirm each module has a single stated responsibility and the entry point remains executable directly.
Confirm npm run check still passes after decomposition with no behavior change.
Confirm the hygiene gate fails on a deliberately introduced violation.

limitations: This audit assesses the 1.0.0 release candidate tree after the eleven findings of AUDIT-2026-08-19-PSO-083 were remediated; that report is superseded.
No hosted CI run, branch protection state, or Actions history was retrieved.
No dynamic analysis, penetration testing, or dependency advisory lookup was performed; the project declares zero runtime dependencies.
MCP server implementations and GitHub-hosted runner images are external and were not evaluated.
No linter or complexity tool is configured, so code hygiene and maintainability were assessed by inspection and by the contract suite.
Adoption and creation were exercised against synthetic fixtures, not against a large production repository.
Skill contract quality was assessed structurally; the runtime behavior of agent-executed skills was not measured.
